2110785275739718049.author: NickBYT_
2110785275739718049.text:
YouTube audiences got bigger and stopped engaging.

Metricool studied 799,718 YouTube videos from 71,177 accounts.

Long-form views went up 76%.

Engagement rate fell 37%, from 3.73% to 2.34%.

That’s the share of viewers who like, comment or share.

Watch time per video dropped too.

More people are watching, and fewer of them care enough to react.

Here’s how to fix it:

Pin a question with two possible answers and say it out loud in the video

Videos that mention the comment section out loud got 34% more comments.

Ask for the subscribe at the end, after the value lands

End-of-video asks performed 1.18x better than the same channel’s videos with no ask.

Post image polls on your Community tab between uploads

Channels that post there consistently get 20-30% more views, and image polls get the most interaction of any post type.

2110415839417835954.author: NickBYT_

10 YouTube habits to start in 2027:

1. Package the video before you film it

Write the title and thumbnail first, the idea decides the views.

2. Follow the rule of 15

In the first 15 seconds, name the problem, give the solution, then raise the stakes.

3. Cover one topic

Channels covering 1 topic get a median 65K views, channels covering 8-10 get 12K.

4. Give your opinion

AI answers any question in seconds, so viewers subscribe for your take on it.

5. Write titles in first person

“I tested” and “I lost” went from below average in 2020 to 20% above in 2026

6. Keep editing minimal

We’re in the authenticity cycle, viewers want to see a real person talking to them.

7. Make videos for the TV

YouTube raised the thumbnail upload limit from 2MB to 50MB for 4K TV screens, so check your thumbnail and text read from across a room.

8. Use one end screen

Send viewers to your most relevant video, or the one with the highest retention.

9. Post image polls on your community tab

Channels that post consistently get 20-30% more views, and image polls perform best of every post type.

10. Use AI for research and editing

Then spend the time it saves being on camera.

2109201716620955959.author: NickBYT_

You should do 5 checks before picking your YouTube niche:

Count active channels

Channels that haven't uploaded in 6 months aren't competing for today's viewers.

Check who’s active and if they’re performing well.

If they are, great there’s demand.

Check what small channels get

Look at channels with 5,000 to 50,000 subs.

If their typical upload clears about 6,800 views, there's real demand for someone your size.

Compare views to subscribers

A typical small channel gets about half its subscriber count in views per video.

If uploads in a niche beat the subscriber count, it's pulling in new viewers.

Be honest about the workload

Quiet niches with big reach usually need slow, expensive videos.

Make sure you can keep up with the niche's pace for a year.

Go one level down

Pick a sub-niche, then study the small channels beating their size before you film anything.

quoted.author: MarioJoos
quoted.text:
YouTube just released a video explaining their algorithm. Here are 50 lessons from this video:

1. YouTube says recommendations are generated based on what it knows about a viewer and their current context. Current context could be factors such as viewing history, time of day, and device type.

2. YouTube says it doesn’t just take a video and try to find an audience for that video. Instead, it starts with a viewer and asks which videos are best for that video at that specific moment.

3. YouTube says a video can have very strong overall metrics (such as ctr and avd) while still being a bad recommendation for a particular viewer.

4. YouTube says a video isn’t initially testing against your subscribers.

5. YouTube says some channels could receive the majority of their viewers from non-subscribers, even shortly after the video being uploaded.

6. YouTube says it can learn that subscribers may not like a video while non-subscribers do.

7. YouTube says it does not decide whether a video is good or bad for everyone based on its early audience response.

8. YouTube says creators tend to overfocus on the first few hours of their analytics. And I couldn’t agree more with this statement.

9. YouTube says a viewer may need to be shown the same video multiple times before they decide to click on it. Often, more than 5 or 6 times even.

10. YouTube says it has experimented with limiting how many times the same video can be recommended to someone.

11. YouTube says context can determine what videos get shown, such as prioritizing a longer video when someone is watching from their TV in the evening.

12. YouTube says its algorithm tries to focus on the long-term value for a viewer.

13. YouTube says there’s no individual metric which determines a video’s success.

14. YouTube says click-through rate often decreases as a successful video reaches a broader audience.

15. YouTube says watch time is important, but doesn’t assume that every minute watched actually represents value.

16. YouTube says it considers both absolute and relative watch time. For those who aren’t too aware of what this means. Absolute watch time is the total amount of time someone spends watching a video, while relative watch time is the total amount of time someone spends watching a video relative to its length.

17. YouTube says satisfaction surveys are used because other metrics alone can’t tell whether viewers actually enjoyed the video.

18. YouTube says, and this one is important, that there’s no universal weighting where one metric has the same importance for every viewer.

19. YouTube specifically recommends looking at retention graphs to understand where viewers are dropping off (You can image how much I smiled when a heard this, for those who don’t know me, I’ve been obsessed with retention knowledge for years)

20. YouTube says turning comments off is not supposed to cause the recommendation system to penalize your videos.

21. YouTube says it tries not to interpret the lack of comments as evidence that viewers don’t like the video.

22. YouTube says the recommendation system is designed not to make decisions based on a single factor.

23. YouTube says turning ads off reduces your video’s reach.

24. YouTube says the algorithm is not trying to assign your entire channel to one topic category.

25. YouTube says it doesn’t deliberately push longer videos simply because it wants longer content getting more views.

26. YouTube says the change in performance for longer viewers is driven by viewer preferences.

27. YouTube believes short-form video became successful because it reduces the decision a person needs to make when choosing what to watch. I’m saying believe because it’s a hypothesis, a hypothesis that I believe is fair to make.

28. YouTube says increasing thumbnail size and showing less videos on desktop increase overall engagement with long-form content.

29. YouTube says it would not have launched the homepage redesign if its experiments had shown that it reduced viewership.

30. YouTube says they’re running hundreds of experiments on the platform at any given moment.

31. YouTube says people sometimes think temporary experiments are permanent changes.

32. YouTube says one off-topic video blowing up does not mean the algorithm is suddenly confused about your channel.

33. YouTube says the decision to create a second channel should be based on whether the content serves the same general audience.

34. YouTube says if two types of content offer different value propositions to different audiences, you should probably consider a second channel.

35. YouTube says its recommendation system can connect audiences between two separate channels when the same viewers watch both channels.

36. YouTube says even when unrelated content is uploaded on the same channel, it can distinguish which videos a viewer may care about.

37. YouTube says a viewer who watched only your short-form videos doesn’t necessarily get your long-form videos recommended. This is in-line with my own findings on viewer conversion being extremely low between formats, often reaching 0.2% or lower.

38. YouTube says a viewer who likes only one topic on your channel, can increasingly only be served that specific topic from your channel.

39. YouTube says creators should plan content around different audience groups instead of assuming their entire audience is one homogeneous group. The way I explain it to creators is: the viewer composition from one video may completely differ from the composition from another video, even though the performance looks the same.

40. YouTube says data from your subscription feed is often better to look at because it's a more controlled subset of your audience. I agree and disagree on this one, because it may also be a limited subset of your audience, so there’s nuance involved with this one.

41. YouTube says viewers regularly watch content from hundreds of channels that have little topical overlap to one another.

42. YouTube says a brand-new channel does not need existing viewer history for its videos to get recommendations.

43. YouTube says it actively tracks whether creators are succeeding and growing through the ecosystem. I can say that they definitely do, sometimes at the benefit of big creators, sometimes at the benefit of smaller creators. 

44. YouTube says it actively tracks whether creators are earning enough revenue to system themselves. This is an interesting one which I haven’t heard them talk about, even in private conversations so I’d be curious to know how they’re doing this.

45. YouTube says bad retention from an external viewing source doesn’t automatically mean that performance should hurt the video on the homepage. This aligns with the advice that you can actually link your content to groups you know for some initial traffic, as long as this group would actually enjoy your content.

46. YouTube says homepage recommendations mainly care about how a video performs in the homepage context. We can actually notice this with shorts. When shorts have better thumbnails, they perform better through browse versus when they don’t have thumbnails.

47. YouTube explicitly gives advice to not disable subscriber notifications in an attempt to improve algorithm performance. They even state that it could prevent connecting your upload to people who would have watched it. Also, at the beginning of the interview they also state that this is the only way to guarantee your content being pushed to your audience.

48. YouTube says subscribing to a channel is a weaker signal of future viewing than most creators assume.

49. YouTube says creators often underestimate how many other channels their own fans regularly watch.

50. YouTube says that you should comment under this post so it reaches more people and so I’m more likely to re-appear in your feed. While I’m half-joking, it does help and my goal is to always spread as much of this information as possible to others. 

Hope you enjoyed this long summary.

Re-uploading clips with no commentary, editing or educational value added.

7. Malicious clickbait

Titles and thumbnails promising what the video never delivers.

This won't always get you suspended but it does hurt your reach.

8. Detection evasion

Editing tricks like mirrored or sped-up footage to dodge YouTube's detection.

Most accounts i've seen get banned?

Or they're not changing up their videos enough.

The first video on a trending topic takes all the distribution.

Study how long it takes your competitors to cover a viral topic in your niche.

2. Stop copying viral videos

There's a difference between copying and spinning off an idea.

YouTube reads all of your content now and has zero reason to push a copy over the original.

So take a viral idea and change the angle or give your take on the viral video.

3. Study runners

Runners are small channels that went viral.

A 10k sub channel pulling 130k views found genuine demand.

Using their video topic for inspiration is one of the easiest ways to go viral. 

4. Sub Niche > Niche

Finance pays $12 to $35 per 1k views.

I recommend every creator starts in a sub niche because they pay more and there's less competition.

5. Write scripts for your own generation

You feel their pain points because they're also yours.

It's the easiest way to build a loyal audience.

6. Idea and Title > everything else

The idea and title are what makes the algorithm push out your video.

So find a viral idea and write the title first.

I see too many creators neglect the 2 things which matter most.

7. Design thumbnails for dark mode

82% of mobile viewers watch YouTube on dark mode.

So make sure your thumbnails are bright and stand out on a dark screen.

8. Use faces

Thumbnails with faces outperform by 143%.

9. Never repeat your title on your thumbnail

The title informs while the thumbnail creates tension.

Saying the same thing twice removes the tension and reduces your CTR.

10. The 15 word rule

Viewers decide to stick around in 5 seconds.

Your first 15 words need to confirm the title, hit the pain point and promise the solution.

11. Open with a bold claim and deliver on it immediately.

12. Close the loop

The biggest retention spike comes when you close the loop your title opened.

So build the video around that moment.

13. Read comments on competitor videos

Comments are where you see what your ideal audience wants.

I've made original viral videos from taking on feedback that was given to my competitors from their audience.

14. Recycle your winners

I hit 71k views, changed the subject and hit 66k with the same format 10 days later.

700k of my views came from that same 1 concept.

15. Post 3 to 7 videos/week

Past 14 and your average views collapse.

16. 5 to 10 minutes is the worst video length on YouTube 

Go 15 to 22 instead.

17. Two channel strategy

Run 2 channels in the same niche with end screens pointing at each other.

Mine boosted subscriber growth +10%.

18. Upload all YT videos to Spotify.

You can post the exact same file, and achieve 2 to 3x YouTube RPM.

19. Don't rely on the algorithm

The algorithm is distribution, never your business.

Build an email list so if something happens to your account, you still own your audience.

20. Post in community tabs

I use community tabs to post polls and carousels.

They've increased my average views by +28%.
